spring.title: Week 12: Sugar Maple, Annika Hansteen-Izora, Walter H. Crockett
spring.subtitle: 7 Days to Vernal Equinox
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

Welcome to maple time, if you live in my corner of North America. The sap of the sugar maple (Acer Saccharum) has been flowing now in most places for several weeks, and the sugar shacks are busy boiling off water to concentrate sugar. Sap runs vary each year in timing and length based primarily on temperature (freezing nights and warming days), though the sap’s sugar content is affected by factors such as the previous summer’s weather. Like with the sap they carry, sugar maple saplings wait to grow until the circumstances are right, and can persist in dense woods for long periods of time until taller trees fall or are removed, at which points they seize the opportunity.

Which is all to say that maple season is a time of contingency and kairos—that is, of indeterminate chances aligning to produce the fullness of time, the ripe moment. Such experiences can feel providential, and we might associate them with, or mistake them for, things like economic opportunity and royal sovereignty, as demonstrated by the first two readings below. But the flipside of contingency and kairos are, as these readings also hint, revolutions (and other “turbulent causes”) and mystery (“certain wonderful chemical processes”). So while maple syrup production might seem similar to the extractive industries that predominate today (fossil fuels, rare-earth metals, digital data, human labor), it is a fundamentally different practice due to the magic of the maple tree—not only its xylem, or sapwood, but the seasonal weaving of nutrients throughout and beyond its parts, from sun and soil to buds and roots through trunk and taps into vats and, maybe, our mouths. Consider this magic, as Hansteen-Izora beautifully writes, among the many “alternative timelines plants offer in their cycles of life and death.” And seize the moment this spring, as the motivational content might say, but also realize that the moment may seize you back.

The maple (Acer) species are part of a large, exciting family (Sapindaceae) known as the soapberries. This family includes the temperate buckeye and horse chestnut—both special trees to me—but also tropical fruit-bearing species such as lychee, longan, rambutan, and ackee.

Readings

  1. The facts related by learned naturalists, botanists, historians, and travellers, and their reflections on the properties and productions of the North American and Canadian Sugar Maple Tree, here presented to the consideration of the reader, cannot fail to interest every nobleman and gentleman possessed of landed property in England, Ireland, and Scotland, and convince them of the certainty of what is here reported[…] The source here presented seems so promising, that if, from revolutions or other causes, all Europe were deprived of foreign sugars, this tree alone, planted in sufficient number, and properly attended to, would supply all its wants; and it may not perhaps be too much to say, that the time may come when that shall take place, either from turbulent causes, or from experience of its convenience and utility.

“Address,” from E. Jones, Review of Facts And Observations, Made by Naturalists, Botanists, Historians, And Travellers, On the Properties And Productions of the Sugar Maple Tree: the Process of Extracting Its Sap, Converting it Into Sugar, &c., &c. (London: E. Colyer, 1832), p. v.

  1. Of all the sweets that man has discovered in a natural state, or has manufactured by processes of refining or blending, the most delicately flavored, the most supremely satisfying to the utmost refinement of taste, is maple syrup. If the figure of speech may be permitted in these days of an ever widening democracy, maple sugar and maple syrup are the reigning monarchs of the blood royal in the kingdom of sweets. […]

    Maple syrup has been called liquid sunshine. To the hard-headed, unsentimental individual, that expression might seem to be an example of the extravagant exuberance of the typical spring variety of poet; but in reality the expression will stand the prosaic test of the scientific laboratory. The sweetness of the sap stored in the maple tree depends in large measure upon the influence of the sunlight upon the leaves of the maple during the summer days preceding the spring sugar season. In some mysterious manner, known only to Nature, the green leaves, under the direct influence of the sun’s rays, store up starch and sugar, and in the laboratory of the maple tree, drawing moisture from roots extending deep down to the marble and granite foundations of the Green Mountains, certain wonderful chemical processes are performed, whereby the sunlight and the water from the mountain springs, and the wholesome ingredients of the soil which give such a superior flavor to the products of Vermont farms and dairies and orchards, unite to make the maple sap out of which the sugar and the syrup are manufactured, that have made the Green Mountain State famous.

“Vermont Maple Sugar,” from Walter H. Crockett, How Vermont Maple Syrup is Made (St. Albans, Vermont: Department of Agriculture of the State of Vermont, 1915), p. 5.

  1. It is in our best interest to question the metronome of capitalism and the ways it arranges time, both structurally and interpersonally. It’s in our best interest to study the alternative clocks that exist. I’m curious about CP time, crip time, Black and Indigenous frameworks of time, pandemic time, jazz constructs of time in the never-ending riff, how time moves with trauma, how time moves with grief, queer time, the alternative timelines plants offer in their cycles of life and death. It’s in our best interest to offer curiosity around ways we can construct our own clocks.

Annika Hansteen-Izora, “Time is Water,” Annika is Dreaming (May 30, 2022).

More

  • Rasheedah Phillips, “Time Zone Generator,” from Time Zone Protocols (2022).

  • Joseph Bruchac, James Bruchac, Jesse Bruchac, and Amy Hook-Therrien, Gluskonba and the Maple Trees (Summertown, Tennessee: 7th Generation, 2024).

  • Abagael Giles, “Warm Nights Bring Some Anxiety for Vermont’s Maple Syrup Makers,” WBUR (March 11, 2026).

  • Nina Foster, “Tradition in Turmoil: Sugar Maple and Climate Change,” JSTOR Daily (March 28, 2025).

spring.title: Week 11: American Robin, Emily Dickinson, Robert Ridgway
spring.subtitle: 14 Days to Vernal Equinox
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

Last week were the first morning bird songs that I have noticed, riding quietly in the car with my partner after dropping our kids at school. I didn’t know it at the time, but that bright morning lay roughly equidistant between the final blizzard of the winter (a nor’easter, as they call it) and a season finale of delicate snow turned into freezing rain. In this way, the cold and warmth, dark and light, liberations and rainy constraints of spring organize this month, as we “interrupt” and “overflow” the patterns of winter yet linger in the “Certainty / And Sanctity” of our hibernations. This transitional season contains a multitude of emotions, as evoked by Dickinson’s other poems featuring Robins (see More below).

The American Robin (Turdus migratorius) is a “true thrush” (genus Turdus) within the general “thrush” (Turdidae) family. Thrushes are passerine, or perching, birds within the order Passeriformes, a highly diverse clade comprising approximately half of the world’s bird species. The American Robin is a migratory bird, unlike its smaller, orange-breasted namesake, the European Robin (Erithacus rubecula), which is classified in the wonderfully named “Old World flycatcher” family (Muscicapidae).

spring.title: Week 13: Paper Birch, Robert Frost, Gifford Pinchot
spring.subtitle: Vernal Equinox
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

Paper birch (Betula papyrifera), also known as canoe birch or American white birch, is a mid-sized deciduous tree native to northern North America. It can be found across the northern half of the continent. Paper birch sap begins flowing near the end of sugar maple season, when daytime temperatures reach above 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and continues to run for only two to three weeks, approximately half as long as maple sap. Although black and yellow birch are more commonly used to produce birch beer, which pairs their sap with wintergreen oils distilled from their bark, paper birch is best for producing syrup or “birch water molasses,” as Cree and other indigenous communities have long done, due to the balanced flavor profile and relatively high sugar content of its sap.

The tree’s wonders go beyond the culinary, touching both art and science. Visually, birches in general are a perennial favorite of painters including Vincent Van Gogh, Gustav Klimt, and Georgia O’Keefe. And the actual bark of the paper birch, in particular, has provided the Anishinaabe with a medium for writing (as wiigwaasabak, a form of scroll), craft, and even transport. The tree’s visual interest and practical applications are due in large part to its high concentrations of betulin—the white, powdery, reflective, and water-resistant substance that gives the bark of the white birches its distinctive appearance. More than just a cosmetic surface, betulin is a bioactive triterpene and the primary natural source of betulinic acid, which scientists are studying for its anti-inflammatory, anti-viral, anti-cancer, and other properties.

Betulin’s protective qualities make the paper birch a sort of superhero tree, allowing it to serve as a ruderal, or early successional species. It arrives first in disturbed and vulnerable landscapes, growing quickly to create a habitat for other trees. Yet the paper birch is also relatively fragile and short-lived, vulnerable to a variety of pests and diseases—and young birch-swingers—with a shorter lifespan than other trees (roughly 80 to 140 years, or shorter in warmer, more humid climates). In the succession of a forest, larger and more durable trees take root under the paper birch and eventually surpass it, outcompeting it for both sunlight and groundwater. The paper birch is “a temporary type of forest,” as Pinchot writes; it soon disappears from the shade it made possible. In the meantime, it grows rapidly, exfoliating bark in horizontal strips as its trunk expands, like a snake shedding its skin.

Readings

  1. Paper birch is an important tree in the Northeast, both for economic and for silvicultural reasons. Its total annual cut is not large in comparison with that of many other species, but it is an important factor in certain wood-working industries. It is used practically to the exclusion of other woods in the manufacture of spools, shoe pegs, shoe shanks, and very largely in the manufacture of toothpicks, dowels, bobbins, shuttles, and various toys and novelties. The fine-grained, even-textured wood is peculiarly adapted to these uses.

    After fires and clearings, paper birch, with aspen, is often the first species to occupy the ground. It takes possession of such areas very readily, restores forest conditions, and furnishes a valuable timber crop. At the same time, it is merely a temporary type of forest, and does not prevent the return of the type natural to the locality.

Gifford Pinchot, “Silvical Leaflets 38: Paper Birch” United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service (October 29, 1908).

  1. I’d like to get away from earth awhile

    And then come back to it and begin over.

    May no fate willfully misunderstand me

    And half grant what I wish and snatch me away

    Not to return. Earth’s the right place for love:

    I don’t know where it’s likely to go better.

    I’d like to go by climbing a birch tree,

    And climb black branches up a snow-white trunk

    Toward heaven, till the tree could bear no more,

    But dipped its top and set me down again.

    That would be good both going and coming back.

    One could do worse than be a swinger of birches.

Robert Frost, “Birches,” Atlantic Monthly (August 1915). Rpt. Robert Frost, Mountain Interval (New York: Henry Holt and Company, 1916), pp. 29-30.

spring.title: Week 18: Great Mullein, Ashia Ajani, Hildegard von Bingen
spring.subtitle: First Quarter Moon; 7 Days to Spring Cross-Quarter Day (May 1)
spring.bodyHtml:
This one’s a day late; I had to catch up on my day job and be an insomniac for a couple nights. Do you have any suggested species or sources for me to include in future dispatches? Leave a comment on Substack or send me an email.

Headnote

The wooly, silver-green leaves were hard to miss in my community garden plot last spring. It’s the sort of plant you’ve seen before but never noticed (cf. “plant blindness”). I decided to let it continue growing, wildly and/or weedily, alongside the plants I had intentionally planted. Eventually, I learned that it was a mullein, likely “common” or “great” mullein, known for centuries as a respiratory support, fish poison, shoe insole, and candle. Plants are full of surprises. But since their introduction to North America up to 400 years ago, mulleins also have been a nuisance for farmers and often treated as an invasive weed. Plants are double-edged swords. Soft shelter or overpowering intruder, symbol of resilience and rage, a cure but also a poison, mullein survives our weeding and may, in the long run, survive us. Its seeds can lie dormant in soil for more than 100 years, until disturbed into the light.

Great mullein (Verbascum thapsus) is one of several hundred flowering species in the Verbascum genus, which itself is in the figwort (Scrophulariaceae) family. This scientific name potentially derives from barbascum (Latin for “bearded”) and Thapsos, the ancient Tunisian city. But the plant’s plethora of enticing nicknames and vernacular titles includes flannel leaf, velvet dock, lady’s candle, hag’s taper, Jupiter’s staff, hare’s beard, donkey’s ear, beggar’s blanket, and—much to my eight-year-old’s delight—cowboy toilet paper. Clearly, its stellate trichomes (star-shaped leaf hairs) and tower-like stem have not gone unnoticed. The biennial plant produces flat rosettes in its first year, followed in year two by a tall spike that flowers irregularly, with each blossom along the spike opening for one day. The spikes remain upright through winter, providing seed and perch or shelter for birds. It is a ruderal species that colonizes fire-scarred or logged landscapes, roadsides and construction sites, and so on. I hope it doesn’t completely overrun my garden.

Readings

  1. One of my favorite facts about mullein is that it can produce hundreds of seeds—and these seeds can lay dormant for decades. I think mullein is clever, and it knows that rage is a conduit. Rage is almost like fire: fire is a reaction. It has to have fuel; it has to have combustion. Fire needs other components to exist. Mullein is like that. The plant produces all of these seeds, but those seeds know, Oh, I’m not in safe ground. Or, I’m not in a good area where I can germinate and grow. I’m going to wait and bide my time.

    Going back to the idea of the Angry Black Woman trope, I grew up going to a predominantly white school. When I did anything there, I was received as angry or full of attitude or sassy. I was constantly trying to prove otherwise—and that became so exhausting. I am okay now. I’m at a place where I’m OK with saying, Hell yeah, I’m angry. Have you seen what’s going on? Why are you not angry?

    Everybody has their own emotions and their own way of processing them. For me, anger is the first emotion that emerges, and then I have to poke behind the anger to see what the real emotion is feeding the anger.

    Anger and grief are very much intertwined for me. I read about the colonial decimation of bison, which facilitated Indigenous genocide in the Great Plains, or I read about a Chinese mining company poisoning a river in Zambia, and I get angry. I get so sad because I’m like, It does not have to be this way. It makes my blood boil seeing what we do to the earth and what we do to each other.

    Colonial powers, Western powers do not treat the earth like a living being; we treat it as something to extract things from. A lot of times that’s how Black people are treated by an oftentimes apathetic population. It’s like, What can we extract from Black people, whether that be labor or culture or inventiveness? That extraction drains us and makes us angry and bitter. If we can have more candid conversations about anger and the way anger shows up in our lives, we would all be better for it.

    Within the canon of ecocriticism and environmental writing, there’s so much talk about sublime beauty and romanticism. Lots of this removes humans from nature, as if the only way nature can be beautiful is without human influence. Amid climate change, we’re seeing more dystopian and post-apocalyptic narratives. I think these perspectives are two sides of the same coin: what does it say when the only way we can think of human engagement with nature is nature punishing us, or us being completely separate from nature? Anger has a place in all of that storytelling.

Ashia Ajani, with Amirio Freeman, “Ashia Ajani Mulls Over Mullein,” PLANTCRAFT (May 5, 2025).

  1. I had an Inflammation of the Bronchial Tube very bad and the phlegm nearly choked me to death. A young man who knows these herbs came to my house and said to me: “If I only knew where there was some Mullein, I could help.” I didn’t know where to get it , and he left , but he came back and this is what he did: Heated the Mullein Leaves in warm vinegar, then put on my neck and chest and later made me drink a cup or two of Peppermint Tea and it helped me very much.

    Writes Mrs. F. N., Mascoutah, Ill.

    Editor’s Note - A knowledge of the medicinal value of herbs will save you many dollars, and much suffering. Our 400-page Herbalist Book describes all American medicinal roots and herbs. It contains color plates and photographic reproductions of hundreds of plants. Price only 25c.

The Old Herb Doctor: His Secrets and Treatments (Hammond, Indiana: Hammond Book Company, 1941), p. 35.

  1. Mullein [wullena] is warm and dry and somewhat cold. Let whoever has a weak and sad heart, cook mullein with meat, fish, or pastry, but without any other herbs, and eat this often; the person’s heart will be strengthened and made happy. Let whoever has a hoarse voice or a sore throat which causes pain in the chest cook mullein and an equal amount of fennel in good wine, strain it through a piece of cloth, and then drink this often. The person’s voice will return and the chest will be healed.

Hildegard von Bingen, from Physica (c. 1150), Hildegard’s Healing Plants: From Her Medieval Classic Physica, trans. Bruce W. Hozeski (Boston: Beacon Press, 2001), pp. 115-116.

spring.title: Week 14: Nimbostratus praecipitatio, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Jenny Odell
spring.subtitle: 86 Days to Summer Solstice
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

If you didn’t know that The International Cloud Atlas exists, then you do now.

First published in 1896 by the International Meteorological Society in France, this trilingual edition codified nearly a century’s worth of taxonomic attention by certain Western European intellectuals, or, shall we say, lay-abouts. Apart from folkloric and indigenous systems of cloud-reading, the scientific classification of cloud formations began right around 1800, when Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and Luke Howard independently developed lexicons in French and English, respectively. Lamarck’s evocative French phrases (i.e., en balayeurs, or broom-like) could not compete with Howard’s Latinate constructions, which won the endorsement of none other than Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who wrote a poem mythologizing the English cloud-gazer. By the time the first Atlas was published, Howard’s romantic pastime had become a gentlemanly institution, housed in national bureaus and eventually international organizations; the project went through many print editions over the next 120 years, before going digital in 2017.

Have I mentioned that springtime can be a polarized, multitudinous season? The mornings are chilled, and the afternoons warm (or vice versa). The ice thaws and leaves behind a trash-filled swamp on the sidewalk. Preemptive acts of undeclared war roil the globe. Rolling rain clouds suffocate the cold lower atmosphere—evoking the “Sad destiny of the troubled world!,” in Goethe’s telling—even as they bring the rain needed to grow new life and, perhaps, discover spiritual transcendence. Cloud-reading is a fitting activity for such a season, with its paradoxical fusion of attention and lethargy, strain and relaxation, precision and imagination. It might reveal to us not only the strange contours of the sky but “the sheer volume of emotions” drifting behind our eyes.

The genus Nimbostratus was first introduced in the 1930 edition of the Atlas because “the definition of nimbus in the Atlas of 1910 led to some confusion” (p. 14, n. 1)—scandalous, I know!1 Due to the formation’s uniform and featureless character, it is not conventionally divided into species. However, the supplementary feature praecipitatio can be appended to the genus when it produces continuous precipitation that reaches the ground (in contrast to virga, referring to precipitation that evaporates mid-air).

Readings

  1. Nimbus
    Now downwards by the world’s attraction driven,
    That tends to earth, which had upris’n to heaven;
    Threatening in the mad thunder-cloud, as when
    Fierce legions clash, and vanish from the plain;
    Sad destiny of the troubled world! but see,
    The mist is now dispersing gloriously:
    And language fails us in its vain endeavour —
    The spirit mounts above, and lives forever.

Goethe, from “In Honour of Mr. Howard” (c. 1820), trans. George Soane and Sir John Bowring, Gold’s London Magazine 4.19 (July 1821), 59-63.

  1. It is possible, even likely, that you’d feel terror, heartbreak, and rage while looking at clouds, at the exact same time that you feel a self-annihilating love of this world. In fact, I would be surprised if, looking at clouds for the first time in a while, many people don’t start crying just from the sheer volume of emotions we can’t allow ourselves to fully feel about what’s happening. To me, it’s so important that that conduit stays open. A fiercely protected capacity for love is, in the end, how we stay alive against the encroachments of cynicism and despair.

Jenny Odell, “What Does It Mean to Watch Clouds? What Can It Mean?” Jenny Odell’s Newsletter (July 4, 2025).

More

  • Thea Applebaum Licht, “Luke Howard’s Essay on the Modification of Clouds (1865),” The Public Domain Review (Dec. 2, 2025).

  • Maria Popova, “89 Clouds: A Poetic Celebration of Clouds and Everything They Mean” (The Marginalian, March 3, 2015). Rev. of Wendy Mark and Mark Strand, 89 Clouds (New York, New York: ACA Galleries, 1999).

  • Richard Hamblyn, The Invention of Clouds: How An Amateur Meteorologist Forged the Language of the Skies (2001; New York: Picador, 2002).

  • Jenny Odell, How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy (New York: Melville House, 2019) and Saving Time: Discovering a Life Beyond Productivity Culture (New York: Random House, 2023).

1

The problem, specifically, was “confusion…between the low, rainy layer resulting from the downward extension of Altostratus and the very low, closely packed clouds (Fractostratus or Fractocumulus of bad weather) which often form beneath the Altostratus or the above-mentioned low layer” (“Preface to the 1939 edition”).

spring.title: Week 16: Ostrich Fern, Martin Heidegger, Douglas Houghton Campbell
spring.subtitle: Last Quarter Moon; 21 Days to Second Cross-Quarter Day (May 1)
spring.bodyHtml:
HEADNOTE

What IS existing?

As German philosopher Martin Heidegger (1889-1976)1 noted, this quintessentially philosophical question might seem “primitive” compared to the specificities of modern science as it defines, dissects, quantifies, calculates, and hypothesizes all things based on empirical observations. Today, we might reframe the question as a riddle about neurons and “consciousness”: does the brain simply generate mental experience (materialism) or somehow channel a universal mind-spirit (idealism)?

Otherwise is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

But for Heidegger, the question of existence was fundamental, and it required a return to ancient ideas, including the pro-Socratic Greek term Physis, or Phusis, derived from the verb phyo (“to bring forth”), and often translated as “nature,” in contrast to Nomos (“law, custom, or convention”). From Physis, we get “physics” as the science of matter and energy. Instead of turning to theorems or mathematical equations, though, Heidegger used this term to refer to our pre-reflective experiences of the world: what we see, feel, touch, or otherwise know before the application of mental interpretations and rational concepts. By postponing cognitive reflection, he attempted to distinguish “beings as such” (the existence of particular cats, people, and objects, which we encounter in physics and other of the natural sciences) from “Being itself” (the presence or revelation of existence in general, as discernible and meaningful to the philosophical tradition of metaphysics). This substratum of existence is not a static substance or representational framework, as modern philosophers sometimes proposed; it is a dynamic event, an unfolding process, through and within which particular beings come to exist or can be encountered as existing. Human “being,” indeed.

Here we’ve entered the realm of strange thoughts, like when we remember that the human body has a resonant frequency, that atoms are quantum clouds of delocalized matter, and that there is a faint glow of ancient radiation saturating the entire observable universe.

This is also the realm of FERNS: primordial (moreso exponentially than even the ancient crocus), flowerless but spore-bearing, tropical-loving and cold-tolerant, sun-optional, sometimes edible, and chaotic to the bone genome. In Aotearoa New Zealand, the unfurling fronds of the tree-like silver fern, or ponga (Cyathea dealbata), embody koru (“loop” or “coil”), a visual leitmotif in art/design representing the emergence of life, the spiral from origin to endless future, and symbolizing the Māori genealogical concept of Whakapapa. Closer to my home, in New England and across the Northern Hemisphere, the ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris) is one of several species whose slow-rocketing croziers, or fiddleheads, mark the return of spring and the persistence of biological life. Both a being as such and a symbol of existence itself, the fern is older, gentler, queerer—and tastier—even than Heidegger’s metaphysics.

The Matteuccia genus is named after Italian physicist Carlo Matteucci (1800–1868), and the struthiopteris species is from the Greek strouthós, “bird,” plus pteron, “wing” or “feather.” The ostrich fern belongs to the small family Onocleaceae, which contains only five species worldwide and is characterized by dimorphism, or the production of two distinct types of frond: tall sterile ones that carry on photosynthesis and give the plant its plumage-like shape, and smaller modified fronds that hold spore-bearing structures through the winter. The former are what can be cooked and eaten. To distinguish the ostrich fern from potentially dangerous lookalikes—particularly the cinnamon fern (Osmundastrum cinnamomeum) and the interrupted fern (Osmunda claytoniana), both of which may cause illness if eaten raw—look for the distinctive deep groove, like a small celery stalk’s channel, running along the inside of the stem. Only the ostrich fern has it.

READINGS

  1. In the age of the first and definitive unfolding of Western philosophy among the Greeks, when questioning about beings as such and as a whole received its true inception, beings were called phusis. This fundamental Greek word for beings is usually translated as “nature.” We use the Latin translation natura, which really means “to be born,” “birth.” But with this Latin translation, the originary content of the Greek word phusis is already thrust aside, the authentic philosophical naming force of the Greek work is destroyed….

    Now what does the word phusis say? It says what emerges from itself (for example, the emergence, the blossoming, of a rose), the unfolding that opens itself up, the coming-into-appearance in such unfolding, and holding itself and persisting in appearance—in short, the emerging-abiding sway. According to the dictionary, phuein means to grow, to make grow. But what does growing mean? Does it just mean to increase by acquiring bulk, to become more numerous and bigger?

    Phusis as emergence can be experienced everywhere: for example, in celestial processes (the rising of the sun), in the surging of the sea, in the growth of plants, in the coming forth of animals and human beings from the womb. But phusis, the emerging sway, is not synonymous with these processes, which we still today count as part of “nature.” This emerging and standing-out-in-itself-from-itself may not be taking as just one process among other that we observe in beings. Phusis is Being itself, by virtue of which beings become and remain observable.

    It was not in natural processes that the Greeks first experienced what phusis is, but the other way around: on the basis of a fundamental experience of Being in poetry and thought, what they had to call phusis disclosed itself to them. Only on the basis of this disclosure could they then take a look at nature in the narrower sense. Thus phusis originally meant both heaven and earth, both the stone and the plant, both the animal and the human, and human history as the work of humans and gods; and finally and first of all, it means the gods who themselves stand under destiny. Phusis means the emerging sway, and the enduring over which it thoroughly holds sway. This emerging, abiding sway includes both “becoming” and “Being” in the narrower sense of fixed continuity. Phusis is the event of standing forth, arising from the concealed and thus enabling the concealed to take its stand for the first time.

Martin Heidegger, An Introduction to Metaphysics (1935), trans. Gregory Fried and Richard Polt (New Haven, Connecticut: Yale University Press, 2000 [1935]), pp. 14–16.

  1. The young leaf grows much more rapidly than the stem, and soon projects beyond it. The multiplication of the cells being greater on the lower side, the leaf begins to curve upward. The cells of the leaf-stalk now elongate rapidly, and after the embryo has broken through the overlying tissue of the prothallium, the leaf pushes up between the lobes of the prothallium, appearing above its surface (Pl. 6, fig. 5).


    The apical cell of the stem divides much more slowly, and follows nearly the same plan at first. The segments later divide somewhat differently, the first division wall of the segment being a radial one, and dividing the segment into two nearly equal cells. The stem is very short at the time the embryo breaks through the prothallium, but the apex is more decidedly conical than is the case in the mature plant.

    The apical cell of the foot soon becomes obliterated by a process entirely similar to that already described, but the cells continue to multiply rapidly with no regular order. By means of the foot, which when complete is large and rounded in shape, the embryo is kept in close connection with the prothallium, and by means of it the embryo is nourished until the first leaf and root are developed.

Douglas Houghton Campbell, The Development of the Ostrich Fern (Boston: Society of Natural History, April 1887), p. 29.

  • Matthew Sharpe, “Heidegger in ruins? Grappling with an anti‑semitic philosopher and his troubling rebirth today,” The Conversation (April 11, 2023).

  • Stacia Brezinski, “Fiddlehead, Ostrich, and Cinnamon: All About Ferns!,” from Maine Audobon (May 6, 2025).

  • Alan Bergo, “Fiddlehead Ferns: Identifying, Harvesting and Cooking,” Forager | Chef (March 14, 2023).

1

Sometimes, two incongruous statements are both true. For example, Heidegger was a wonderfully earnest nature mystic and poet-philosopher. He was also a wretched Nazi stooge, and his attempt to recover a dynamic, organic notion of existence from pre-Socratic philosophy was tangled up in reactionary Folkist mythologies of soil and blood, as well as his own spiritualized admiration for the Third Reich. Arguably, the contemporary right-wing appropriation of Heidegger, the related rise of eco-fascisms around the world, and the “creep” of these ideas into mainstream environmentalism and popular culture make it all the more crucial to engage with and understand his ideas now.

spring.title: Week 15: Dutch Crocus, Guillaume Barth, William Herbert
spring.subtitle: Waning Gibbous Moon; 28 Days to Second Cross-Quarter Day (May 1)
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

The crocuses likely have already come and gone. They can return each spring almost too early, before the snow melts, before the robins return, before the atmosphere warms (let alone the soil). Here in my urban neighborhood, the Dutch crocus (Crocus vernus) blooms in tandem with the snowdrops (Galanthus nivalis) and just prior to the daffodils (Narcissus pseudonarcissus). These corm-based geophytes, which require 10 to 15 weeks of cold to biochemically shift their apical meristem, or growing point, from leaf- to flower-production, have become such a seasonal marker for me that I assumed they must be native to this landscape. And maybe they are—now. But their journey to here crosses several continents and centuries, through the studios of Dutch painters and the apothecaries brewing saffron concoctions to treat the Black death, across the slopes of the Alps and the diplomatic circuits of Holy Roman ambassadors, originating primarily from the grassy hillsides of Anatolia, the species’ primary center of diversity.

These are ancient origins. John Milton pictured the crocus embroidering the ground of Eden, “more colour’d than with stone / Of costliest emblem,” and the other poets, of course, love the flower’s evocative timing and physical form. Ovid and other Greeks recorded a more tragic tale about Crocus’ place within the empire of flowers. Though long associated with the cradle(s) of civilization, the saffron crocus (Crocus sativus), source of the world’s most expensive spice, now is being cultivated across New England, all the way out to Provincetown.

Otherwise is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The Crocus genus is part of the trimerous iris family (Iridaceae) but is distinct from the true Iris genus. The Dutch, or spring, Vernus species is one of several that bloom in spring, coming after the precocious tommasinianus (woodland) and chrysanthus (snow), alongside flavus (yellow), and long before the autumn group that includes sativus (saffron) and the beautiful but toxic crocus imposters of family Colchicaceae. Of particular note: the saffron crocus is a mutant or hybrid that contains three sets of chromosomes and is therefore sterile; it has survived as a clone for more than 3500 years through the division and propagation of corms by human hands, and its thread-like stigmas are also still harvested by hand, as they were in Minoan civilization.

Readings

  1. C. vernus is one of the most widely extended Croci, and of the easiest culture, producing seeds abundantly, which, as neither the birds nor the mice seem to eat them, become almost a nuisance from the multitude of self-sown seedlings, which come up spontaneously, and intrude where they are not wanted. It is the Crocus of the Alps, but its flower is small there, promiscuously purple and white or whitish, generally with the throat purple on the outside, but always white and hairy within. It reaches Cevennes; and I am told it is to be found, though rare, on the Pyrenees. Brotero states it to be found in the north of Portugal, but his plant is perhaps C. Carpetanus. It extends, with white acute flowers, into Carinthia, and is found white, with very blunt obovate flowers, on the Bavarians Alps, sometimes assuming a blush of purple. I believe it is only found in particular spots on the Pyrenees, affecting the oolite or Jurassic limestone. On the Alps it reaches above 5000 feet of altitude. I have seen it both white and purple from the Tyrol. The finer purple Neapolitan variety inhabits the loftiest mountains of Calabria and Lucania, not descending lower than 5000 feet. On Monte Pollino it flowers as late as June and July, reaching an elevation of 6000 feet. On the Wengern Alp its flowers actually pierce the remaining snow in June.

William Herbert, A History of the Species of Crocus, ed. John Lindley (London, England: William Clowes and Sons, [1847]), pp. 25-26.

  1. In his installation Crocus sativus, fleur du bonheur, Guillaume Barth pays homage to the saffron flower by capturing the moment of its birth. The artist invented a rotating plate system for time-lapse photography so as to reveal the rotating movement of the flower, like the dance of the dervishes for which it is a metaphor. It opens under the full moon and blooms for 24 hours, which is the duration of its life. A video projects this actual size in the middle of a levitating circle with a diameter of four metres. Visitors are invited to stand on a rug whose motif recalls the spiralling form of the petals. There they hear a melody inspired by the root sounds of Sufi tradition, composed by Mirtohid Radfar. The three phases in this music sing the rising of the saffron flower from its bulb, the exaltation of its opening, and then a gentle settling. It sets forth the present moment. There are three circles: the rotating movement of the flower, the circle of the carpet and, above all, the undulating field of the music spinning around us and within us. This multicultural work offers a space of resilience. Known since time immemorial, saffron is a powerful natural anxiolytic associated with joy, luck and regeneration.

Gallery text from Guillaume Barth, Crocus sativus, fleur du bonheur (Studio National des Arts Contemporains du Fresnoy, 2021).

  • Janis Ruksans, Crocuses: A Complete Guide to the Genus (Portland, Oregon: Timber Press, 2011).

spring.title: Week 17: Eastern Cottontail , Zora Neale Hurston, Ernest Thompson Seton
spring.subtitle: New Moon; 14 Days to Spring Cross-Quarter Day (May 1)
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

Few creatures are more storied than the rabbit and its cousin, the hare. Their manifestations extend across the globe, ranging from cosmology and folklore (Nanabozho and Br’er Rabbit) into transatlantic children’s literature (Lewis Carroll’s “White Rabbit,” Peter Rabbit, and Peter Cottontail), and onward to twentieth-century cartoons (Bugs Bunny, Roger Rabbit) and cinematic riddles (the eponymous Harvey and Donnie Darko’s Frank)—let’s not get into the other versions of bunnies in American pop culture. Across their many forms, these leporine figures embody a variety of traits and entities: transformation and trick; the moon and its goddess, or perhaps the underworld; fertile abundance or skittish cowardice—unless you are Monty Python and the medieval symbolism that inspired those British flapdoddlers. The symbols are appropriately numerous for the famously procreative creature.

My kids have excitedly spotted several individual rabbits in our urban neighborhood this spring (no fluffles yet), including one parent-shaped Easter bunny. I like to think the kids and the rabbits share a special connection, as both introduce a mix of docile dependence and feral wildness into the adult- and concrete-dominated cityscape. Remembering these tender wildlife sightings, or cross-identifications, it is a bit bewildering to dig up the wealth of rabbit-related scientific imagery and taxonomical data available in the public domain. So much energy and precision expended, much of it at public expense (back when that happened), to see and to understand. Yet this perspective is not neutral. As much as it reflects the wonders of science and of dedicating research for the public good, rather than corporate intellectual property, it also demonstrates how long-lasting, how granular was the American colonial project of mapping and quantifying the continent’s natural resources for the purposes of controlling and potentially extracting value from them. Millions upon millions of rabbits killed, initially for food and fur, and later for pest control. No longer our kin, and no longer a source of sustenance or myth, the rabbit lives on at the edges of our gardens and digital media, a tender blessing, a possible threat—yes, still a trickster.

The Eastern Cottontail (Sylvilagus floridanus, formerly known as Lepus sylvaticus) is the most common rabbit throughout New England and one of the most frequently found mammals across the continent. The species includes as many as 25 subspecies, varying primarily by region. In the northeast, the Eastern Cottontail has outcompeted the native New England Cottontail (Sylvilagus transitionus), which has smaller eyes, darker fur, slightly shorter ears with black edging, and often a black spot between its ears. The Eastern Cottontail is more versatile and adaptable than its New England kin, which relies on dense underbrush—maybe even briar patches—for protection. It roams into forest clearings, open meadows, and even suburban yards, relying instead on electric explosions of energy to leap away from harm. Rabbits and hares are both in the order Lagomorpha, along with the exceedingly adorable pika (genus Ochotona) and the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), from which contemporary domestic rabbits descend.

Readings

  1. … Well, de ‘gator was a pretty white varmint wid coal black eyes. He useter swim in de water, but he never did bog up in de mud lak he do now. When he come out de water he useter lay up on de clean grass so he wouldn’t dirty hisself all up.

    So one day he was layin’ up on de grass in a marsh sunnin’ hisself and sleepin’ when Brer Rabbit come bustin’ cross de marsh and run right over Brer ‘Gator before he stopped. Brer ‘Gator woke up and seen who it was trompin’ all over him and trackin’ up his pretty white hide. So he seen Brer Rabbit, so he ast him, “Brer Rabbit, what you mean by runnin’ all cross me and messin’ up my clothes lak dis?”


    Brer Rabbit was up behind a clump of bushes peerin’ out to see what was after him. So he tole de ‘gator, says: “Ah ain’t got time to see what Ah’m runnin’ over nor under. Ah got trouble behind me.”

    ‘Gator ast, “Whut is trouble. Ah ain’t never heard tell of dat befo’.”

    Brer Rabbit says, “You ain’t never heard tell of trouble?”

    Brer ‘Gator tole him, “No.”

    Rabbit says: “All right, you jus’ stay right where you at and Ah’ll show you whut trouble is.”

    He peered ‘round to see if de coast was clear and loped off, and Brer ‘Gator washed Brer Rabbit’s foot tracks off his hide and went on back to sleep agin.

    Brer Rabbit went on off and lit him a li’dard knot1 and come on back. He sat dat marsh afire on every side. All around Brer ‘Gator de fire was burnin’ in flames of fire. De ‘gator woke up and pitched out to run, but every which a way he run de fire met him.

    He seen Brer Rabbit sittin’ up on de high ground jus’ killin’ hisself laughin’. So he hollered and ast him:

    “Brer Rabbit, whut’s all dis goin’ on?”

    “Dat’s trouble. Brer ‘Gator, dat’s trouble youse in.”

    De ‘gator run from side to side, round and round. Way after while he broke thru and hit de water “ker ploogum!” He got all cooled off but he had done got smoked all up befo’ he got to de water, and his eyes is all red from de smoke. And dat’s how come a ‘gator is black today—cause de rabbit took advantage of him lak dat.

Zora Neale Hurston, Mules and Men (1935; New York: Harper Perennial, 1990), pp. 106-107.

  1. WINTER DENS
    In cold winter, the Cottontail is seldom found in a form or bed, unless it be very well sheltered. She much prefers a hole under a stone pile, a hollow log or tree, at such times. She uses these for more than mere snoozing places, as we shall see. Indeed, she would not be true to rodent tradition if she did not at some time assume the deathlike torpor that may be called a “cold sleep.” A driving storm sets in. Molly is ensconced under a thicket of briers and fern in one of her best forms, one most nearly weatherproof. The snow heaps up, shutting her into a sort of crystal-white cavern. Deeper and deeper piles the snow. Then the temperature falls, so that, though protected, she is numbed into a sort of frozen sleep. The raging of the storm outside kills every desire to venture forth. So long as the blizzard lasts, she rests, cold but not unhappy; a little hungry, perhaps, but not frozen—only drowsy—so drowsy that the easiest thing is to “lay low” and wait for better days.
    […]
    TAMABILITY
    It is a curious fact in the history of wild things that many of the wildest become most completely tame when properly managed; and many of those that, in their native state, are half-tame, can never be made domesticated or docile. Thus, the superferal Elephant, Wild Horse, Wild Dog, Wild-cat, Mink, Antelope, falcon, wild duck, respond completely when taken young, become members of the family. But the half-tame Fox, Hyena, pheasant, Canada jay, wood duck, and Cottontail, have never yet been tamed. They may be taken young and brought up so they tolerate our dwellings and our company, but never do they become truly members of the household-that is, domesticated—never do they learn to come at call, and rejoice in our company; never do they elect to stay with us when given the choice of returning to their wildwood kindred.

Ernest Thompson Seton, Lives of Game Animals, Volume IV, Part II: Rodents, Etc. (Garden City: Doubleday, Doran, and Co., 1929), p. 806, 807.

Supplementum

  • Joshua J. Mark, “Manabozho Tales,” World History Encyclopedia (February 12, 2025).

  • Anne C., “Rabbits in Myth and Legend,” shelftalk: The Seattle Public Library Blog (October 6, 2009).

  • Zora Neale Hurston, “The Eatonville Anthology,” The Messenger 13.11 (November 1926): 332.

  • J.A. Allen, Monographs of North American Rodentia. No. 2.—Leporidae, United States Geological Survey of the Territories (Washington: Government Printing Office, 1877).

spring.title: Week 19: Sheet Moss, Hildegard von Bingen, Michael Marder
spring.subtitle: Full Moon; Second Cross-Quarter Day
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

If there’s a plant that reminds me of God, it’s probably moss. Indeed, the plant’s biology is as ornate and rarefied as any systematic theology. Ubiquitous and abundant but amorphously changing, obvious but mysterious, perennially surprising and yet easy to take for granted, expanding or contracting as it slowly transforms its surroundings—modest moss can be as soft as the tender, mighty mullein, but its diminutive, hair-like roots, called rhizoids, work over time to accomplish feats of erosion that would be impossible for other plants. Moss is slow green fire, breathing air, water, and minerals into its pseudoparts; and permitting a multitude of traditional and experimental applications, from bedding, wound-dressing, and whiskey-making to biofuels and pharmaceuticals. For example, because of their nearly immediate interchange with the atmosphere, these subtle sculptors also function as bioindicators in both wild and human-developed landscapes, reflecting the quality of the air and capable of detecting even microplastics and trace elements of heavy metals.

The full-spectrum greens of the mosses embody the viriditas (“greening power” or “greening life-force”) that medieval mystic Hildegard of Bingen identified as God’s vital presence suffusing earth, soul, and cosmos. In her dynamic elemental visions, consuming-illuminating fire and blowing-atmospheric wind converge to draw moisture into dry soils, bodies, and souls, bringing forth plants and fruits, growth and strength, virtuous acts of faith and hymns of praise. Although May and its first day are conventionally a time of flowers—the Roman festival of Floralia, the circling garlands and symbols of the maypole, and the month of Floréal on the French Revolutionary calendar—for me this is a month of mosses. Look to the decaying ground and the rocky crevices for a soft brush with the Creator.

Otherwise is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The Hypnum genus, classified in the Hypnales order of “leafy” or “feather” mosses, is known for its thick, carpet-like growth and vivid green, yellow, or brown colors. These branching, mat- and tuft-forming species are pleurocarpous (pleura, “side,” plus karpos, “fruit”), in contrast to upright, capsule-bearing acrocarpous varieties. The Hypnum genus includes an undetermined number of species (in the range of hundreds), but all are part of the 11,000+ “true mosses” in the class Bryopsida. This class excludes several hundred varieties of moss (e.g., peat and granite mosses), which have various distinct characteristics, as well as outright imposters such as Spanish moss (related to the pineapple) and Irish moss (a seaweed). Along with liverworts (Hepaticopsida) and hornworts (Anthocerotophyta). all mosses are bryophytes in the Bryophyta division. These non-vascular, moisture-dependent plants lack true roots, stems, and leaves but are crucial for soil development and water retention. And the Victorians sure did love to press them under magnifying glasses.

Readings

  1. How could any creation of Mine be void and useless? For every creature that lives (even those without the powers of reason or sensation) has two useful properties within itself, and one that perishes. The two useful ones are its juiciness or sap and its green foliage, but the other part withers in its dryness. The human being also has two components, that is, the soul and the body— the soul in virtues, the body in action— but it also knows evil, which is arid like the part that perishes.

Hildegard of Bingen, “334. Letter to Secular People” (circa 1153), Letters of Hildegard of Bingen: Volume 3 (New York: Oxford University Press, 2004), p. 136.

  1. Why is our conceptualization of time, drawing on metaphysical order and stability, ineffectual when it comes to the time of moss? First, as we have seen, the relative terms young and old, before and after, are inapplicable there where a linear chronology breaks down. Second, the paradigm of energy gradually dissipating in the measure of distancing from an energetically rich beginning no longer works when faced with moss: diminished vitality coincides with the exuberance of mossy vegetal life, one that infinitely mirrors and is mirrored in “the architecture of the forest.” Third, though “primitive,” moss encompasses at least fourteen thousand species and includes virtually all methods of plant reproduction (be they sexual or asexual) and growth, reliant on mutual interactions with the boundary layer or the microclimate that surrounds each leaf and growing point of every plant. Hence, already, in the nineteenth century, a relevant entry in The Edinburgh Encyclopedia stated: “He who could examine the nutrition, the growth, the regular confirmation, the provision made for the continuation of the species…of even the minutest Phascum [mosses], without perceiving in them proofs of intelligence, power, and goodness, would probably receive no more conviction from the sublimest truths that astronomy can unfold.” Finally, moss grinds rocks to stand and builds up soil for future plant growth; it performs simultaneously the tasks of analysis and synthesis, complicating the (mythical) image of time as a universal destroyer, the merciless devourer of all without exception.

Michal Marder and Edward S. Casey, Plants in Place: A Phenomenology of the Vegetal (New York: Columbia University Press, 2024), p. 76.

  1. Along with lichens, bryophytes are often the first actors in primary succession: the ecological process of weathering bare rock into soils that can sustain more complex forms of life. This can occur after a volcanic eruption or the retreat of a glacier; here in New England, mosses and lichens are still waging a battle against the bare rock of our highest peaks. Once established, bryophytes modify their environment through cation exchange. In this process, a bryophyte releases a proton (H+) from its cell walls into the surrounding environment, which in turn displaces positively charged ions (cations) such as calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), and potassium (K⁺) from nearby soil or rock particles. The bryophyte then absorbs these essential nutrients into its tissues.

“Mosses of Maine: A Brief Guide,” Oxford County CTS (October 15, 2025).

  • Ellen McHale, “7 Interesting Things About Mosses,” Kew Royal Botanic Gardens (May 23, 2020).

spring.title: Week 20: Cambridge Argillite, Ludwig Wittgenstein, The Dana Brothers
spring.subtitle: Waning Gibbous Moon; 44 Days to Summer Solstice
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

It’s worth at least checking your bedrock. You may find a surprising history beneath your feet.

As for me and my apartment, the story goes something like this:

A while back, when the continents were arranged much differently, the bedrock of present-day Boston was adrift on the Iapetus Ocean as part of a microcontinent called Avalonia. More or less a chain of volcanic islands, Avalonia had split off from the supercontinent of Gondwana together with parts of what are now the UK and northern Europe. When all dry land on the planet eventually converged into the mother of all continents, Pangaea, the islands of Avalonia were crushed between the tectonic plates of Baltica (Europe) and later Laurentia (North America). So they rested until Pangea broke apart, and the Atlantic Ocean rifted Avalonia into two parts: New England and parts of Canada to the west, and old England and parts of Europe to the east.

The fault line where Avalonia fused to Laurentia is visible in a few places across Massachusetts, including the so-called “Bloody Bluff” in Lexington. The land to the east of this bluff, where I live, shares rocks and fossils and other subtle features with the hills of Wales and other regions across the wide ocean. So while the flora and fauna of surrounding Boston may be part of North America, the region’s bedrock originated from another continent entirely. We live atop strange layers of time and stuff; but as Wittgenstein notes below, sometimes what we are looking for is less the facts of the matter than the knowledge that they exist.

As a sedimentary rock, Cambridge Argillite likely was formed off the coast of Avalonia, when a combination of underwater currents and submarine mudslides laid down thick layers of fine-grained silt in what eventually would become the Boston basin. This mud was later buried, compacted, and lightly metamorphosed, creating a dense grey rock (or sometimes purplish-grey) that looks like shale but breaks into irregular chunks rather than thin sheets. Such characteristics created many headaches when they were digging the subway tunnels under my current apartment. But Cambridge Argillite also provides a generally stable foundation for heavy urban infrastructure, and has conductive properties that make it suitable for shallow geothermal applications, including under my kids’ school. Rock on.

Readings

  1. “How am I able to obey a rule?”—if this is not a question about causes, then it is about the justification for my following the rule in the way I do.

    If I have exhausted the justifications I have reached bedrock, and my spade is turned. Then I am inclined to say: “This is simply what I do.”


    (Remember that we sometimes demand definitions for the sake not of their content, but of their form. Our requirement is an architectural one; the definition a kind of ornamental coping that supports nothing.)

Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations, trans. G.E.M. Anscombe (Oxford, England: Basil Blackwell, 1953), §217 (p. 85).

  1. Its colours are grey and red. Of grey, it occurs bluish grey and blackish grey; these are disposed sometimes in stripes or spots; and of red, it occurs brownish purple red. The surface is sometimes rendered beautifully pavonine, irised and chatoyant from the presence of Oxide of Iron.

    Its lustre is glimmering.


    It is opaque.


    It is amorphous.


    The streak is pearl grey.


    It is moderately hard.


    The fracture is fine grained uneven , passing in some specimens, into imperfectly straight foliated, and in others into earthy, and it is always slaty.


    It is moderately tough.


    It is easily frangible.


    The fragments are tabular and splintery, and often perfectly

    rhomboidal.


    Its specifick gravity is about 2.888.

James Freeman Dana and Samuel L. Dana. “Argillaceous Slate,” from Outlines of the Mineralogy and Geology of Boston and its Vicinity, with a Geological Map (Boston: Cummings and Hilliard, 1818), p. 57.

spring.title: Week 21: Common Lilac, Amy Lowell, Ronald Firbank
spring.subtitle: Waning Crescent Moon; 37 Days to Summer Solstice
spring.bodyHtml:
Headnote

The lilac—so pure, so sweet, so artificial. Although only 20 to 25 species of lilacs exist in the wild, more than 2,000 named cultivars (according to the official International Lilac Registrar) have been developed, most over the past 150 years. Beginning in the 1870s, French botanists Victor and Marie Louise Lemoine began using needles, tweezers, and paintbrushes to delicately cross the common lilac—native to the Balkan Peninsula but common throughout Europe—with species from China and other regions, creating spectacular double-flowered and early-blooming hybrids. Other breeders around the world followed suit, leading to an explosion of new varieties, actual plants, and public interest. The numerous cultivars now require a color code for reference and classification: I (White), II (Violet), III (Blue), IV (Lilac), V (Pink), VI (Magenta), and VII (Purple)—with some European organizations also recognizing VIII (Creamy Yellow.)

The flowers are just as abundant in literary and musical texts, featuring prominently in poems by Walt Whitman, Amy Lowell (see below), and even Hannah Arendt; short stories by the wonderful Kate Chopin and the lesser-known Aleksandr Kuprin; prose by Henry David Thoreau and Marcel Proust; and, of course, in various renditions of the sultry, melancholic ballad, “Lilac Wine.” If mosses are divine, then lilacs are carnal.

The common lilac (Syringa vulgaris) is a flowering deciduous shrub in the olive family (Oleaceae). This family, which includes approximately 28 genera and 700 species, such as olive, ash, jasmine, and forsythia, is grouped in the order of mints (Lamiales, not to be confused with the specific mint family, Lamiaceae). And this order is characterized by several features: (1) paired rotating leaves—or “opposite decussate phyllotaxis,” in botanical terms; (2) bilateral, two-lipped flowers that are fused into a tube; (3) reduced reproductive organs, including two or four stamens; and (4) strong scent oils concentrated in microscopic glandular hairs, or trichomes, that blanket the leaves and stems. Of course, lilacs differ from this final trait in concentrating their volatile scent oils exclusively within their flowers, replacing the general defense mechanism of the mints with a targeted, highly volatile aromatic lure for spring pollinators—“sweet and heady,” indeed.

Readings

  1. Lilacs,

    False blue,

    White,

    Purple,

    Color of lilac.

    Heart-leaves of lilac all over New England,

    Roots of lilac under all the soil of New England,

    Lilac in me because I am New England,

    Because my roots are in it,

    Because my leaves are of it,

    Because my flowers are for it,

    Because it is my country

    And I speak to it of itself

    And sing of it with my own voice

    Since certainly it is mine.

Amy Lowell, “Lilacs” (The New York Evening Post, 1920), rpt. What’s O’Clock (Boston: Houghton Mifflin Company, 1925), pp. 68-74.

  1. In May when the lilac is in flower, admiration is expressed for it on every side; even the most indifferent observer cannot restrain himself from manifesting his appreciation of the flower, praising its beauty and expressing a wish that it might be employed more frequently than it is in garden work. The gardener realizes that in this shrub we have particularly valuable material for gardens and parks, and recently unusual interest has been taken in it. Great collections, embracing hundreds of varieties, have been planted at the Arnold Arboretum in Boston, and at Highland Park in Rochester. This year at Highland Park, when the lilacs were at their best, they were inspected by over 30,000 visitors in one day, who had only words of appreciation and admiration for them.

William C. Barry, The Lilac (Rochester, NY: Mount Hope Nurseries), p. [2]. Rpt. from Horticulture (Oct. 9, 1909).

  1. Offering a light, lilac wine, sweet and heady, Miami circled, here and there. She had a cincture of white rose-oleanders, and a bandeau of blue convolvoli. She held a fan.

    “Or do you care for anyt’ing else?” she was enquiring, automatically, of Mr. Musket (the Father of three very common girls), as a melodious tinkle of strings announced the advent of the minstrels from Broken Hill.

    Following the exodus roadward, it was agreeable to reach the outer air.

    Under the high trees by the yard-door gate, the array of vehicles and browsing quadrupeds was almost as numerous as upon a Market day. Coming and going between the little Café of the “Forty Parrots” (with its Bar, spelled Biar in twinkling lights), the quiet village road was agog, with bustling folk, as perhaps never before. All iris in the dusk, a few loosely-loinclothed young men, had commenced dancing aloofly among themselves, bringing down some light (if bitter) banter from the belles.

    Pirouetting with these, Miami recognized the twinkling feet of her brother Charlie, a lad who preferred roaming the wide savannah country after butterflies with his net, to the ever-increasing etiquette of his home.

Ronald Firbank, Sorrow in Sunlight (London: Brentano’s Ltd., 1924), pp. 27-28.

  • David Doochin, “The Unknown French Horticulturist Who Made Lilacs Happen,” Atlas Obscura (June 28 2016).

spring.title: Week 22: Mycobacterium vaccae, Jenifer Wightman, Graham A.W. Rook
spring.subtitle: Waxing Crescent Moon; 30 Days to Summer Solstice
spring.bodyHtml:
This week goes long on history and biology—the latter not my forte. Bear with me as I venture into the science of the small. The surprising story is worth it.

Headnote

They’re in the soil. You may have heard that a single teaspoon of soil contains tens of billions of individual microorganisms—far more than the total population of currently living humans, and perhaps approaching the total number of humans who have ever walked this planet. Indeed, recent research suggests that more than half of all species on Earth dwell primarily beneath our feet, in the microcosmos of infinitesimal life. And common among these tiny dirt dwellers are some very interesting and important “old friends” that we humans should get to know better: bacteria, parasites, and other microbes (viruses, fungi, and protozoa) that offer many known and potential benefits to humans.

In his 1665 book, Micrographia, English scientist Robert Hooke produced a striking illustration of the fruiting structures of “blue mould” (something in the genus Mucor), thereby offering humans our first glimpse of the microscopic realm. When the eccentric Dutch experimentalist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed bacteria in 1676, he referred to the amusing little things he observed squirming in water as “animalcules.” Scientific wonder at these tiny forms grew into public fear roughly two centuries later, when the germ theory of disease gradually replaced belief in miasmas, and biologists realized that bacteria were responsible for horrifying diseases such as tuberculosis and leprosy.

By the beginning of the twenty-first century, though, things have come full circle. We now know that bacteria and other microorganisms, even viruses and parasites, operate as an “invisible organ,” hidden body, or “second human genome” within us, playing many crucial roles: digesting complex carbohydrates, producing essential vitamins, educating our immune systems, and shielding the body from harmful pathogens. We are, in fact, holobionts. Microbes also play crucial roles outside of our bodies, in agriculture and food preparation, industry and biotechnology—microscopic cyanobacteria, after all, generated the planet’s breathable atmosphere. How did we get here?

In 1971, immunologists noticed that people living near Lake Kyoga in central Uganda responded better to the vaccine for leprosy than people in other regions of the world. They connected this vaccine response to a strain of Mycobacteria vaccae (from vacca, Latin for “cow,” from which, via cowpox, we also get the word vaccine).1 This bacteria was so abundant in the local environment that it lent a bright orange-yellow tint to the mud surrounding the lake. Thus began a radical revision of modern germ theory. The existence of good germs means that sterility is not synonymous with health; and while hygiene is still crucial, so is biodiversity—not just out in nature, but around us and inside us.

When later researchers tested Mycobacteria vaccae as an immunotherapy for lung cancer patients, they were surprised to find that, although treatment did not extend the patients lives, it significantly improved their mental health. Why this unexpected side effect? Follow-up studies identified the specific mechanism, revealing that exposure to the bacteria stimulated serotonin production and helped regulate stress responses in mice. The notion of a “dirt antidepressant” made headlines, further research confirmed the near-immediate benefits of direct contact with plants and soil, and wellness entrepreneurs rushed to commoditize yet another miracle-promising supplement. Pardon me if I go do some weeding in my garden instead.

Mycobacterium vaccae is a nonpathogenic bacteria commonly found in soil around the world. It is a saprophyte, or saprotroph, meaning that it feeds off of decaying matter, secreting enzymes to break down dead organic matter or waste and absorbing whatever nutrients emerge. This bacteria has extensive immunoregulatory and anti-inflammatory properties that are being explored; and, through microbial prospecting, a strain of it can even be used to find oil. The Mycobacterium genus includes several infamous disease-causing species, including those responsible for tuberculosis and leprosy. But other mycobacteria are being studied for potential medical and health applications, ranging from treatment of cancers (Mycobacterium obuense) and allergy-induced asthma (Mycobacterium phlei) to remediation of polluted soils (Mycobacterium chitae). After a week of perusing the bacterial universe, I feel that I’ve only scratched the surface.

Readings

  1. Bacteria are the original synthesizers. Although bacteria are simple single cell organisms, they are a biological force adapting to and accessing minute resources in severe climates such as the Arctic or the deep sea. This adaptability has made bacteria the most genetically diverse and abundant (in mass and number) organisms. In their chemical and physical resource cultivation, they impact both their micro and macro ecosystems. On the macro scale, for example, bacteria generated oxygen stores that contributed to the creation of the ozone layer. The ozone layer was critical in reducing harmful effects of sunlight on evolving DNA. Bacteria also created greenhouse gases to warm the earth so that the climate was ripe for evolution of higher organisms. Even now, bacteria are profound players in the contemporary terrestrial economy.

    Bacteria thrive if conditions are favorable; they mutate, migrate, die, or lie

    senescent if conditions are not favorable. They consume, reproduce, deplete their resources, and release waste products. As bacteria express themselves (i.e. live), they alter their habitat. They synthesize new environments or landscapes, thereby producing new ecological niches for other organisms. As such, they offer a field for mapping the rhythms and patterns constitutive of life.

Jenifer Wightman, “Winogradsky Rothko: Bacterial Ecosystem as Pastoral Landscape.” Journal of Visual Culture 7.3 (December 2008: 309-334), p. 312.

  1. Which organisms from the natural environment are important in addition to those from animals? Although there is no direct evidence linking soil consumption to health benefits, it is evident that soil is a significant source of microbial exposure in natural settings. Soil microorganisms become airborne in dust during dry conditions, but also when raindrops impact the soil, because tiny explosions of soil organisms occur, releasing them into the air. Additionally, soil organisms settle on food, particularly in farmers' markets where washing and packaging are minimal. Moreover geophagy (consumption of soil) is an evolved behaviour. It is probable that all vertebrates, especially in early life, engage in it, and the green iguana is a well-studied example of this. Many primate species, including gorillas, orangutans, and chimpanzees have been observed eating soil. Geophagy is a common practice in many cultures, and is frequently observed during pregnancy, not only in underdeveloped rural societies but also in Western cultures where it is often considered a pathological manifestation of pica. Many of the Treg-inducing and immunoregulation-enhancing strains of bacteria are found in soil.

Graham A.W. “The Old Friends Hypothesis: Evolution, Immunoregulation and Essential Microbial Inputs.” Frontiers of Allergy 4 (September 12, 2023), p. 8.

  1. Context Inflammation is increasingly recognized as contributing to the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (MDD), even in individuals who are otherwise medically healthy. Most studies in search of sources for this increased inflammation have focused on factors such as psychosocial stress and obesity that are known to activate inflammatory processes and increase the risk for depression. However, MDD may be so prevalent in the modern world not just because proinflammatory factors are widespread, but also because we have lost contact with previously available sources of anti-inflammatory, immunoregulatory signaling.

    Objective To examine evidence that disruptions in coevolved relationships with a variety of tolerogenic microorganisms that were previously ubiquitous in soil, food, and the gut, but that are largely missing from industrialized societies, may contribute to increasing rates of MDD in the modern world.

    […]

    Conclusion Measured exposure to the old friends or their antigens may offer promise for the prevention and treatment of MDD in modern industrialized societies.

Charles L. Raison, Christopher A. Lowry, and Graham A.W. Rook. "Inflammation, Sanitation, and Consternation: Loss of Contact With Coevolved, Tolerogenic Microorganisms and the Pathophysiology and Treatment of Major Depression." Archives of General Psychiatry 67.12 (December 2010): 1211–1224.

Supplementum

  • “Getting Dirty May Lift Your Mood,” University of Bristol (April 2, 2007)."

  • Lisa Marshall, “Stalking the Dirt Vaccine.” Colorado Arts and Sciences Magazine (The University of Colorado Boulder: September 28, 2018).

  • Chris Lowry, “The Old Friends Hypothesis & the M. Vaccae Story.” The Microbiome Summit (2019).

  • “Soil Quotes,” U.S. Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service (n.d.).

  • Antoni Van Leeuwenhoek, “Observations, communicated to the publisher by Mr. Antony van Leewenhoeck, in a dutch letter of the 9th Octob. 1676. here English'd: concerning little animals by him observed in rain-well-sea- and snow water; as also in water wherein pepper had lain infused.” Philosophical Transactions R. Society 12.133 (March 25, 1677): 821–831.

1

In 2018, the Lake Kyoga strain was reclassified as a distinct species, Mycobacterium kyogaense. This sort of thing seems to happen a lot with bacteria.
