summer.title: Week 33: Perseids, Han Dynasty Scribes, Henry David Thoreau
summer.subtitle: The annual summer shower that has been running for eons
summer.bodyHtml:
Waxing Crescent Moon - 14 Days to Full; 39 Days to Fall Equinox

Headnote

At the risk of this becoming an extraterrestrial blog, I am continuing last week’s astronomical theme as we exit the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. Although it offers no liquid relief to the summer heat, this shower is a long debris trail with an equally long tale to tell.

Our dear little planet is peppered by Perseids around the same time every year, although the timing fluctuates slightly due to calendar mechanics and the wobbling of the Earth’s axis, gradually shifting later in the year at a rate of approximately 1.5 days per century. And the shower is replenished every 133 years, when the Swift-Tuttle comet again enters our inner solar system from the distant Kuiper Belt and crosses Earth’s orbit on the way to its perihelion (closest point to the sun). As it passes through our neighborhood, the 16-mile-wide comet sheds some of its frozen gases, rock and mineral debris, and carbon compounds, leaving a renewed debris trail for our planet to spin through.1 The comet’s last visit to the sun was in December 1992, and it won’t return again until July 2126 (nearly 100 years from today). In the meantime, though, in 2028, we will pass through an especially rich “filament” of dust shed by the comet in 1479, which is expected to amplify the annual shower into an outright meteor storm.

The first recorded observation of the Perseids shower was made in China nearly 2,000 years ago, in the extensive manuscript annals of the Han Dynasty (202 BCE to 220 CE), and was preserved for centuries through the region’s dedicated manuscript culture. This ancient observation was first compiled and translated for European audiences in 1841, as part of a French text presented below for your decoding pleasure. Yes, this took me a while to track down and verify, even with the help of a chatbot. But it was, I submit, worth it to encounter that ancient scribe’s evocative turns of phrase, transmitted to us across continents, millennia, and media forms.

Humans didn’t really figure out how meteor showers and shooting stars worked, including the regularity of their timing, until the nineteenth century. Prior to that, some Catholic cultures in Europe referred to the Perseids shower as the “tears of St. Lawrence”; the feast day of this martyred saint—who is supposed to have told the people burning him to death, “This side is cooked enough; turn me over and eat!,” thereby securing his spot as the patron saint of both cooks and comedians—falls on August 10th. It wasn’t until 1838 that New Haven bookseller (and future Yale librarian) Edward C. Herrick more fully connected the dots across several years and, eventually, much of recorded history. This was the era that recognized meteors as more than just transient atmospheric phenomena, unrequiring of further study; for example, amateur British astronomer W. F. Denning first documented, in detail, how the Perseids shower gradually moves across the sky as Earth passes through the comet debris.

Now, with those millennia of accumulated attention and eventual documentation behind us, humans in the twenty-first century can watch a state-sponsored live-stream of Perseids on Youtube and poetically chronicle “this vertiginous awareness / mocking gravity on our speck of now.” The infrastructure of our attention runs deep.

Readings

  1. 36. Période Khien-wou, 12e année, 1re lune, jour ki-oueï (9 février), on vit de petites étoiles filantes au nombre d’un cent au plus : les unes allaient au N. O. d’autres allaient directement au N. et d’autres au N. E. Après deux nuits, ce phénomène cessa.—A la 6e lune , jour wou-yn (27 juin), au lever du jour, on vit une centaine de petites étoiles filantes allant vers les quatre points cardinaux; elles étaient semblables à un peuple nombreux qui émigre. A la 10e lune , jour ting-mao (14 octobre ou 13 décembre), on vit une grande étoile filante , très-lumineuse, qui partit de l’astérisme Tsing (μ, γ, ε, ζ, Gémeaux), se dirigea de l’orient à l’occident, et fit un grand bruit.


    [36. Xianwu period, 12th year, 1st month, jiwei day (February 9): about a hundred small shooting stars were seen; some moved toward the northwest, others directly north, and others toward the northeast. This phenomenon ceased after two nights. — In the 6th month, wuyin day (June 27), at daybreak, about a hundred small shooting stars were seen moving toward the four cardinal points; they resembled a vast migrating crowd. In the 10th month, dingmao day (October 14 or December 13), a large, very bright shooting star was seen; it originated from the Jing asterism (μ, γ, ε, ζ, Gemini), traveled from east to west, and produced a loud noise.]

Edouard Biot. Catalogue Général Des étoiles Filantes Et Des Autres Météores Observés En Chine Pendant Vingt-quatre Siècles. Paris: Impr. royale, 1841. 138. [Trans. courtesy of Google; emphasis added.]

  1. The poet must be continually watching the moods of his mind as the astronomer watches the aspects of the heavens. What might we not expect from a long life faithfully spent in this wise? The humblest observer would see some stars shoot. A faithful description as by a disinterested person of the thoughts which visited a certain mind in threescore years and ten, as when one reports the number and character of the vehicles which pass a particular point. As travellers go round the world and report natural objects and phenomena, so faithfully let another stay at home and report the phenomena of his own life — catalogue stars, those thoughts whose orbits are as rarely calculated as comets. It matters not whether they visit my mind or yours — whether the meteor falls in my field or in yours — only that it comes from heaven. (I am not concerned to express that kind of truth which Nature has expressed. Who knows but I may suggest some things to her? Time was when she was indebted to such suggestions from another quarter, as her present advancement shows. I deal with the truths that recommend themselves to me — please me — not those merely which any system has voted to accept.) A meteorological journal of the mind. You shall observe what occurs in your latitude, I in mine.

Henry David Thoreau. “August 19, 1851.” Journal, Vol. II: 1850 - September 15, 1851. Ed. Bradford Torrey. Boston, Massachusetts: Houghton Mifflin and Company, 1906. 403.

But the correlation isn’t ironclad: Jupiter’s gravity continually reshapes the trail.

summer.title: Week 35: Cucumis, Robert Hass, Marcus Aurelius (and William Cowper, too)
summer.subtitle: A fast-climbing sprawler birthed on multiple continents that is mostly water
summer.bodyHtml:
Waning Gibbous Moon — 13 Days to New; 24 Days to Fall Equinox

Headnote

Which is messier, the history of words or of plants?

Something like "squash" is exactly what it claims to be. The English word was adopted from the Narragansett word, askutasquash ("the things that may be eaten raw"), from askut, "green, raw, uncooked," plus asquash, "eaten." Compare that to “kabocha,” the sweet-fleshed winter squash beloved across Japan, which derives its name from a compression of the Portuguese Camboja abóbora, "Cambodia pumpkin.” It was assigned this name merely because Cambodia happened to be the last port Portuguese sailors called at before reaching Japan. This particular squash is not Cambodian, or even really Asian, since every member of the genus Cucurbita, including kabocha, traces its origins to the Americas.

Cucumber's confusion works in a different way. While Kabocha's name wandered from the truth, cucumber's name never moved at all—but the plant beneath it did. This is the namesake of the genus Cucumis, home to both true cucumbers and many sweet melons since Linnaeus devised his system of botanical classification in 1735. When the Roman historian Pliny described the “cucumis” grown for Emperor Tiberius, who demanded a daily serving of the crisp, refreshing fruit (did I mention that cucumbers and melons are, botanically, berries?); and when the Mishnah described the downy “qishu’im” eaten in second-century Judea, later translators rendered both terms as “cucumber.” But true cucumber (Cucumis sativus) is smooth and warty, not downy. The hairy, twisted, serpentine fruits these ancient writers describe in fact match the ancient Egyptian snake, or chate, melons (varieties of Cucumis melo—not yet the sweet melons we know today, which wouldn't emerge in Central Asia for another several centuries). These crisp, high-water-content melons arrived in Europe centuries before the cucumber. Only gradually did true cucumbers replace these melons in European art, writing, and mouths,1 as they journeyed from the foothills of the Himalayas across the Indo-Mediterranean world through two routes: overland through Persia into northern/Eastern Europe and, later, across the Mediterranean via Islamic trade and agriculture. Thus, the long history of the word “cucumber,” which possibly stretches back to ancient Sumer, was extended a little further.

When this wanderwort, or “wandering word,” eventually arrived in the English language, “cucumber” replaced the Germanic eorþæppla (literally, “earth-apples”) but spent several centuries being pronounced as “cowcumbers”—perhaps, according to one folk legend, because they were primarily considered a bovine treat. Once the word was introduced to the Americas, however, its range again expanded to include not only true cucumbers (rumored to have been brought there by Christopher Columbus) but many other cucumber-like fruits, including those from Africa (Cucumis anguria, aka the maroon cucumber or West Indian gherkin), Europe (the aforementioned Cucumis melo var. flexuosus, or snake melon), and the Americas themselves (Echinocystis lobata, or wild cucumber; and Marah macrocarpus, or Cucamonga manroot).

Cucumber’s taxonomical bedfellow, “melon,” seems to sidestep this messy history. The word comes from Latin melo, shortened from melopepo, which was borrowed from the Greek mēlopepōn ("apple-gourd"). Like “squash,” “melon” named what it saw and left it at that: no mistranslated ancestor, no wrong continent. Linnaeus's decision to lodge melon inside the same genus as cucumber was based on their substantial similarities: their vining morphologies, monoecious flowers, and pepo-like fruits (a hard rind surrounding a fleshy, many-seeded interior). Yet his decision had repercussions appropriate to the messy Cucurbits family. In 1988, a group of researchers proposed splitting the genus so that cucumbers kept their longstanding name, while melon and its relatives would be exiled to a new genus called Melo. The proposal never took, and when genetic sequencing finally arrived to settle the matter, it didn't divide the family; it further enlarged it, absorbing five more genera just to maintain the category’s phylogenic coherence. In the process, the genus's assumed geography was extended, too, as Cucumis turned out to have an entire overlooked branch stretching through the Malay Archipelago and into Australia.

The names reach, split, and tangle like the vines themselves. Yet their humble refreshment—musky sweet, or vegetal and slightly bitter—persists.

Readings

  1. In the old torment of the earth
    When the fires were cooling and disposing themselves
    Into granite and limestone and serpentine and shale,
    It is possible to imagine that, under yellowish chemical clouds,
    The molten froth, having burned long enough,
    Was already dreaming of release,
    And that the dream, dimly
    But with increasingly distinctness, took the form
    Of water, and that it was then, still more dimly, that it imagined
    The dark green skin and opal green flesh of cucumbers.

Robert Hass. From “Poem with a Cucumber in It.” The American Poetry Review 36.5 (September/October 2007): 34.

  1. A cucumber is bitter.⁠—Throw it away.⁠—There are briars in the road.⁠—Turn aside from them.⁠—This is enough. Do not add, And why were such things made in the world? For thou wilt be ridiculed by a man who is acquainted with nature, as thou wouldst be ridiculed by a carpenter and shoemaker if thou didst find fault because thou seest in their workshop shavings and cuttings from the things which they make. And yet they have places into which they can throw these shavings and cuttings, and the universal nature has no external space; but the wondrous part of her art is that though she has circumscribed herself, everything within her which appears to decay and to grow old and to be useless she changes into herself, and again makes other new things from these very same, so that she requires neither substance from without nor wants a place into which she may cast that which decays. She is content then with her own space, and her own matter and her own art.

Marcus Aurelius. Meditations, Book VIII, Section 50. Circa 175 CE. The Thoughts of The Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. Trans. George Long. Boston, Massachusetts: Little, Brown, and Company, 1899. 209.

  1. To raise the prickly and green-coated gourd,
    So grateful to the palate, and when rare
    So coveted, else base and disesteem'd —
    Food for the vulgar merely — is an art
    That toiling ages have but just matur'd,
    And at this moment unassay'd in song.
    Yet gnats have had, and frogs and mice, long since,
    Their eulogy; those sang the Mantuan bard,
    And these the Grecian, in ennobling strains;
    And in thy numbers, Phillips, shines for aye
    The solitary shilling. Pardon then,
    Ye sage dispensers of poetic fame,
    Th' ambition of one, meaner far, whose pow'rs,
    Presuming an attempt not less sublime,
    Pant for the praise of dressing to the taste
    Of critic appetite, no sordid fare,
    A cucumber, while costly yet and scarce.

William Cowper. From “The Task, Book III: The Garden. 1785. The Poetical Wrks of William Cowper. Ed. William Benham. London: Macmillan and Co., 1870. 446-462.

autumn.title: Beach. Rose. Hips.
autumn.bodyHtml:
Now that fall is officially here, I’m remembering fondly the floral, citrusy taste of the rose hip tea I made in August.

The blossoms and subsequent pods did not seem as abundant along the beach as in previous years, perhaps because of my timing or because of the widespread drought across New England this summer. But I was still able to collect a few handfuls of decent quality and ripeness.

It’s easy to quarter and boil the hips and press them through a mess strainer. In the past, I’ve added sugar to make a conventional syrup for mixed drinks. This year, I used a smaller quantity of water to try for a more concentrated liquid. My batch of hips was quite spiky and seedy, but the result, for whatever reason, was less soapy on the tongue then my attempt last year.

The taste was very late summery to me, as I combined it with juice (mainly in seltzer format) and made a few gin-based cocktails. I’m no expert when it comes to mixing drinks, but it was a fun and refreshing little experiment. And because rose hips are so high in vitamin C, I told myself that this little potion was doubling as a pre-autumn immunity boost.

Here’s hoping I can manage some more foraging adventures this fall and winter.

winter.title: Week 10: Witch Hazel, Friedrich Nietzsche, William Hamilton Gibson
winter.subtitle: 21 Days to Vernal Equinox
winter.bodyHtml:
To any stray readers of this intermittent project, which I am now calling by a new name:

Welcome to Lectio Terra, a weekly series of curated readings drawn from botany, philosophy, and related disciplines. We are roughly 10 weeks past the winter solstice and closing in on the vernal equinox. Join me in this solar cycle for some eccentric, esoteric, ephemeral fun.

Otherwise is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Headnote

When witch hazel blooms in late fall or early winter, it surprises our sense of time and place. I haven’t witnessed its dried seed pods exploding, as Gibson describes humorously later in his reflection. But I remember once, perhaps my first encounter with the plant, finding yellow ribbons of witch hazel unfurled under piles of snow and thin globes of ice. The plant’s strange time-keeping can remind us to look again at dormant life and feel something different in the cold air. The title of Nietzsche’s essay collection, “untimely meditations,” has been translated as “thoughts out of season.” In that spirit, may witch hazel be an “encouragement,” as Nietzsche writes, “to live after our own rule and measure.”

Vernal witch hazel (Hamamelis vernalis) is native to the Ozarks rather than New England, but it is noteworthy for its bright and sometimes fragrant late winter blooms, in February through early March, alongside Chinese, Japanese, and hybrid varieties—such as the “Arnold Promise” cultivar created, accidentally, by Boston’s own Arnold Arboretum . Common witch hazel (Hamemelis virginiana), which is native to New England, blooms in late autumn. The witch hazel genus (Hamamelis) is related to the winter hazel genus (Corylopsis), native to Asia, and to other genera within the controversial Hamamelidaceae family.

Readings

  1. October 20th - One by one the lingering wild flowers have succumbed to the frosts; a few of the hardy asters being the only reminders of the regal glory of the October copses. But though the blighting breath of the approaching winter is fast quenching even these remnants of bloom, there is one fresh blossom which shall abide to welcome “chill November,” even as the dandelion welcomed May, and as the rose and the golden-rod welcomed June and September. The waving pennants of the witch-hazel, coiled for weeks within their patient buds, are now swung out from thousands of gray twigs in the copses, and the underwoods are lit up with the yellow halo from their myriads of fringy petals.

“The Witch Hazel Bombardment,” from William Hamilton Gibson, Sharp Eyes: A Rambler’s Calendar (1892; New York: Harper & Brothers, 1904), p. 230.

  1. But even if the future leave us nothing to hope for, the wonderful fact of our existing at this present moment of time gives us the greatest encouragement to live after our own rule and measure; so inexplicable is it, that we should be living just to-day, though there have been an infinity of time wherein we might have arisen; that we own nothing but a span’s length of it, this “to-day,” and must show in it wherefore and whereunto we have arisen. We have to answer for our existence to ourselves; and will therefore be our own true pilots, and not admit that our being resembles a blind fortuity. […] The true educators and moulders reveal to thee the real groundwork and import of thy being, something that in itself cannot be moulded or educated, but is anyhow difficult of approach, bound and crippled: thy educators can be nothing but thy deliverers. And that is the secret of all culture: it does not give artificial limbs, wax noses, or spectacles for the eyes—a thing that could buy such gifts is but the base coin of education. But it is rather a liberation, a removal of all the weeds and rubbish and vermin that attack the delicate shoots, the streaming forth of light and warmth, the tender dropping of the night rain; it is the following and the adoring of Nature when she is pitifully-minded as a mother;—her completion, when it bends before her fierce and ruthless blasts and turns them to good, and draws a veil over all expression of her tragic unreason—for she is a step-mother too, sometimes.

“Schopenhauer as Educator,” from Friedrich Nietzsche, Untimely Meditations (1873-1876), pp. 105-106, 107-108.
